x: On 21 June the Tropic of Cancer has about 13.5 h of daylight, the Arctic Circle 24 h and the Equator about 12 h.

s: What happens to days in the Northern Hemisphere from 23 September to 21 December?
x: In this period northern days shorten while southern days lengthen; the reverse happens from December to March.

s: When are day and night approximately equal?
x: An equinox is a seasonal transition with about equal day and night; a solstice has unequal day and night and maximum seasonal contrast.

s: Around which date does the winter solstice occur in the Northern Hemisphere?
x: The northern winter solstice is around 22 December and the autumnal equinox around 22 or 23 September.

s: The International Day of Yoga is observed on which date, which also corresponds to the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
x: The International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June, the date of the Northern Hemisphere’s summer solstice.

s: What does the North Pole experience on 22 December?
x: The North Pole has continuous night at the December solstice, continuous day at the June solstice and sunrise or sunset at an equinox.

s: On 23 September, over which latitude is the Sun overhead?
x: On 23 September (and 21 March) the Sun is overhead at the Equator.

s: What does the Southern Hemisphere have on 21/22 December?
x: On 21/22 December the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day; on 21 June the Northern Hemisphere does.

s: During the March Equinox, which season begins in the Southern Hemisphere?
x: At the March Equinox spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere and autumn in the Southern Hemisphere.

s:
Arrange the following critical positions of Earth in chronological order during a year:
A. September Equinox
B. June Solstice
C. December Solstice
D. March Equinox
x: The order is March Equinox, June Solstice, September Equinox, December Solstice, that is D, B, A, C.

s: Which of the following pairs about the June solstice is NOT correctly matched?
o: Northern Hemisphere – Longest day and shortest night
x: At the June solstice the North Pole has continuous daylight, not darkness.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: 21 March – Sun overhead at the Equator, moving northward
21/22 December – Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer
21 June – Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, starting to move southward
23 September – Sun overhead at the Equator, moving southward
x: On 21/22 December the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, not Cancer.

s: When the North Pole has six months of continuous daylight, what does the South Pole have?
x: Axial inclination and revolution give the poles opposite six-month patterns of day and night.

s: What does the Arctic Circle experience on 22 December?
x: On 22 December the Arctic Circle has 24 hours of night; on 21 June it has 24 hours of day.

s: What is the period from 22 December to 21 June, when the Sun appears to move northward, called?
x: Uttarayana is the Sun's apparent northward movement from 22 December to 21 June.

s: Which of the following cities has the shortest day on 21 June?
x: On 21 June day length grows northward, so the southernmost city, Thiruvananthapuram, has the shortest day.

s: At the December solstice, over which latitude is the Sun overhead?
x: At the December solstice the Sun is over Capricorn; at the June solstice over Cancer; at the equinoxes over the Equator.

s: On which dates is the Sun vertically overhead at the Equator?
x: The Sun is overhead at the Equator twice a year, at the equinoxes of 21 March and 23 September.

s: What was the theme of the International Day of Yoga 2026?
o: Yoga for One Earth, One Health
x: The 2026 theme of the International Day of Yoga (21 June, summer solstice) was 'Yoga for Healthy Ageing'.

s: Which latitude has a 12-hour day throughout the year?
x: Only the Equator has equal day and night (12 hours) all year.

s: On 22 December, about how long is the day at the Tropic of Cancer?
x: The Tropic of Cancer has about 10½ hours of day on 22 December and about 13½ hours on 21 June.

s: In which month does the Southern Hemisphere have its shortest day?
x: The Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around 22 December and its shortest around 21 June.

s:
Arrange the following cities in decreasing order of day length on 21 June:
1. Delhi
2. Kanyakumari
3. Srinagar
4. Hyderabad
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: On 21 June day length grows northward: Srinagar > Delhi > Hyderabad > Kanyakumari.

s: During the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere, which pole is tilted towards the Sun?
x: During southern summer, the South Pole is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.

s: Why do more oblique solar rays produce lower heating?
o: Spread the same energy over a larger area
x: Oblique rays spread the same energy over a larger area, so heating per unit area is lower.

s: Why does the summer hemisphere receive greater heating than the winter hemisphere?
o: It is nearer to the Sun
Its solar rays are more direct and its days are longer
Its solar rays are more oblique
x: Direct rays and longer days give the summer hemisphere more heating.

s: Which of the following describes the summer hemisphere?
x: The summer hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, getting concentrated energy, a higher Sun and longer days.

s: Which of the following pairs (season – feature) is correctly matched?
x: In summer the Sun is higher and shadows shorter; winter has oblique rays and shorter days.

s: Which season does the Northern Hemisphere experience when it is tilted towards the Sun?
x: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets more direct rays and longer days, producing summer.

s: Which of the following is NOT a factor affecting the distribution of insolation?
o: Angle of incidence of solar rays
x: The major factors listed are the angle of incidence, duration of day, atmospheric transparency and land configuration. Direction of ocean tides is not one of them.

s:
Consider the following statements about the distribution of insolation:
1. Maximum insolation is always received at the Equator.
2. Insolation generally decreases from the tropics towards the poles.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
x: Insolation generally decreases from the tropics to the poles; subtropical deserts with cloudless skies can receive the maximum, so the Equator is not always the maximum zone.

s: Where is maximum insolation received?
x: Insolation is highest over cloudless subtropical deserts, not the Equator.

s: Which latitude zone experiences the greatest seasonal differences in day length and insolation?
x: Seasonal differences are greatest in high latitudes because the annual swings in day length and insolation are very large there.

s: In which regions are four distinct seasons generally experienced?
x: Mid-latitudes show four distinct seasons; low latitudes have wet and dry periods and subtropics hot summers and mild winters.

s: What type of seasons do the low latitudes mainly experience?
o: The largest swings in day length
x: Low latitudes have small temperature contrast and wet and dry seasons; four distinct seasons belong to the mid-latitudes.

s: Which is the hottest month of summer in the Southern Hemisphere?
x: The Southern Hemisphere's summer peaks in January, its hottest month.

s: Why does Christmas fall in summer in Australia?
o: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere
Australia is nearest the Sun in December because of its longitude
x: In December the Southern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, so Australia has summer at Christmas.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Lower Sun in the sky – Shorter shadow
Higher Sun in the sky – Longer shadow
Vertically overhead Sun – No shadow at noon
Midnight sun – No shadow at noon
x: An overhead Sun casts no shadow at noon; a higher Sun gives a shorter shadow, a lower Sun a longer one, and the midnight sun is the Sun visible above the horizon at midnight.

s:
Consider the following statements about the overhead noon Sun:
1. Only places between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn can receive it.
2. Delhi, lying north of 23½°N, receives it once a year.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Only places between the two Tropics get the overhead Sun; Delhi, north of 23½°N, never does, so statement 2 is wrong.

s: On 21 June, where is the noon shadow absent because the Sun is overhead?
x: On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so an object there casts no shadow at local noon.

s: Lying between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer, how often can Andhra Pradesh receive the overhead noon Sun?
x: Andhra Pradesh (about 12°41′N to 19°07′N) lies between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer, so the overhead Sun can occur there twice a year.

s: Where was a temperature of about 50°C recorded in 1935?
x: About 50°C was recorded at Ganganagar in 1935, during the March-May hot weather season.

s: Under the IMD's seasonal classification, which season follows the South-West monsoon?
x: IMD's four seasons run winter, pre-monsoon, South-West monsoon and post-monsoon.

s: In which months is the noon shadow absent at the Equator?
x: The Sun is overhead at the Equator at the March and September equinoxes, so there is no noon shadow then.

s: Which of the following cities never has the Sun overhead at noon?
x: Only places between the Tropics get the overhead Sun; Srinagar lies north of 23½°N.

s: How many ritus (seasons) are there in the traditional Indian calendar?
x: The traditional calendar has six ritus, from Vasanta to Shishira.

s: About what share of Andhra Pradesh's rainfall comes from the South-West monsoon?
x: The South-West monsoon (June–September) brings about two-thirds of AP's rain.

s: Which layer of the atmosphere is called the 'Ozonosphere'?
x: The stratosphere holds the ozone layer and so is called the Ozonosphere.

s: What are the days called when the noon Sun is overhead at a place between the Tropics and objects cast no shadow?
x: Places between the Tropics get the overhead noon Sun twice a year; these are called zero-shadow days.

s: Which is the coldest place in Andhra Pradesh?
x: Lambasingi is the coldest place in AP (about 2°C), not the hottest.

s: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of the Earth's axial tilt?
o: Unequal length of day and night
Location of the polar circles at about 66½°

s: Vega was the pole star about 14,000 years ago and will be again in about 12,000 years. What is the reason?
o: The slow wobble (precession) of Earth's axis
x: Earth's axis slowly wobbles (axial precession), changing the direction of the celestial pole; Vega was the pole star about 14,000 years ago and will be again in about 12,000 years.

s: What are the long-term orbital and axial variations that influence climate collectively known as?
x: Long-period variations in Earth's orbit and axial behaviour that influence climate are called Milankovitch cycles.

s: Seasons occur because of the Earth's revolution combined with which of the following?
x: The axial tilt changes the Sun's angle and day length as Earth revolves, producing seasons.

s: Why does the Earth's axis keep approximately the same orientation during its revolution?
x: Angular momentum keeps the axis parallel to itself; opposite seasons are a result of this, not its cause.

s: At what angle is the Earth's axis inclined to the plane of its orbit?
x: The axis makes 66½° with the orbital plane, which is a 23½° tilt from the perpendicular.

s: What is the line on the Earth that divides day from night called?
x: The circle of illumination divides the lit half of the Earth from the dark half.

s: Because of the Earth's rotation, in which direction does the Coriolis force deflect winds in the Northern Hemisphere?
x: The Coriolis effect deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

s: How does melting ice that shifts mass away from the Earth's axis affect its rotation?
x: Mass moving away from the axis slows the Earth's rotation.

s: Which combination most accurately explains the seasonal variation in the angle of incidence of solar rays and the length of day?
o: Rotation alone and changing distance from the Sun
Ocean currents, tides and the changing speed of winds
Axial inclination, parallelism of the axis, revolution and the spherical shape of the Earth
The elliptical orbit alone and the rotation of the Moon
x: Seasonal variation results from the Earth’s axial inclination, the parallelism of its axis, its revolution around the Sun and its spherical shape. These alter the Sun’s angle and the duration of daylight received by different regions.

s: What mainly causes the seasons on the Earth?
x: Seasons come mainly from axial tilt affecting solar angle and day length; Earth is in fact nearest the Sun during northern winter.

s: At what angle is the Earth's axis inclined to the plane of its orbit?
x: The axis is 23½° from the perpendicular, which is 66½° to the orbital plane.

s: Which of the following is NOT a cause of the seasons?
x: Rotation causes day and night, not seasons; seasons come from axial inclination, parallelism and revolution.

s: Towards which star does the Earth's axis keep pointing during its revolution?
x: By parallelism the axis keeps pointing towards the Pole Star throughout the revolution.

s: Around which date is the Earth at perihelion, nearest the Sun?
x: Perihelion falls around 3 January; aphelion, the farthest point, is in early July.

s: Which season does the Northern Hemisphere have when the Earth is nearest the Sun?
x: Earth is nearest the Sun (~3 January) during the northern winter, so distance cannot cause seasons.
